question.text: Vindhya Event-Driven Fund (Cat III) is evaluating a peer-group benchmark drawn from a commercial hedge-fund index that only includes funds currently reporting. The portfolio-construction team at the fund's investment committee flags a specific bias that inflates the benchmark's average return. Which bias is this?

answer.text: Self-reporting bias — only well-performing funds volunteer data
Strategy heterogeneity — funds with different mandates are pooled together
Backfill bias — new funds add historical returns selectively on joining the index
Survivorship bias — funds that closed, liquidated, or stopped reporting are excluded from the index history

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Survivorship bias arises specifically because funds that liquidated, merged away, or stopped reporting (often due to poor returns) are dropped from the historical series. The remaining 'survivor' set has an upward-biased average return. HFRI, Credit Suisse/Tremont, Eurekahedge, Barclay Hedge all wrestle with this. It is distinct from self-reporting bias (voluntary reporting skew) and backfill bias (selective backdating of history). **The Trap:** Self-reporting (Option A) and backfill (Option C) are real biases, but the specific mechanism described — excluding funds that stopped reporting — is the textbook definition of SURVIVORSHIP bias. Strategy heterogeneity (Option B) is a peer-construction issue, not an index-bias mechanism. **Cross-Exam Context:** XIX-B (Cat III Distributor) and XIX-C (All-Cat Manager) also test hedge-fund index biases. Cat I/II AIFs face different measurement issues (valuation staleness / NAV smoothing) — not survivorship in the same form. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** When presenting hedge-fund peer benchmarks to your Cat III investment committee, always ask the data vendor whether the index is 'live-only' or 'dead-fund-inclusive.' A 200-400 bps annualised lift is typical when survivorship is not corrected — it makes your relative alpha look worse than it is.
